passage: Several of the indigenous writing systems used in West Africa can each be traced to a single inventor. The syllabary devised for the Vai language of present-day Liberia, first documented in the 1830s, is attributed to Momolu Duwalu Bukele. Beginning in 1896, Ibrahim Njoya, king of Bamum in what is now Cameroon, developed a script that changed over the next fourteen years from a collection of pictographic symbols into a syllabary of eighty characters. And in the late 1980s, brothers Ibrahima and Abdoulaye Barry of Guinea invented Adlam, an alphabet for transcribing the Fulani language.

options: It traces the decline of several West African languages, then describes efforts to preserve them in writing.
It makes a general observation about some writing systems, then gives examples that bear it out.
It identifies the creator of one script, then explains how that script shaped the development of others in the region.
It notes that a region has produced many scripts, then describes how most of those scripts fell out of use.

passage: Navajo textile artist Melissa Cody, who grew up watching her mother and grandmother at the loom and began weaving at age five, works in what is known as the Germantown Revival style. On a traditional Navajo loom built by her father, she weaves tapestries whose vibrant colors, diamond patterns, and overlapping geometric forms seem to rise off the surface in three dimensions. Alongside traditional Navajo symbols, Cody often includes personal tributes and references to pop culture.

It introduces a weaver, then describes the distinctive features of the tapestries she creates.

passage: Because the archaea in a sediment core taken from the Arctic seafloor near Loki’s Castle, a hydrothermal vent field, belonged to groups never grown in a laboratory, microbiologists Anja Spang, Thijs Ettema, and colleagues sequenced the DNA extracted directly from the sediment and pieced together genomes from the fragments. One previously unknown lineage, which they named Lokiarchaeota, turned out to be more closely related to eukaryotes, the organisms whose cells contain a nucleus, than any archaea previously known. The finding strongly supports the idea that the eukaryotic cell arose from an archaeal ancestor that already had many of the genes on which eukaryotic complexity depends.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It explains how researchers identified a new group of microbes, then considers what the discovery suggests about the origin of complex cells.
It outlines a method for growing microbes in a laboratory, then describes the organisms that the method allowed researchers to study.
It recounts the collection of a seafloor sample, then explains why the organisms it contained could not be classified.
It reports a discovery made near a hydrothermal vent, then raises doubts about how other scientists have interpreted that discovery.

passage:
The following text is from Anne Bradstreet’s 1678 poem “The Author to Her Book.” The speaker addresses a book of her poems, which was printed without her approval, as though it were her child.

Yet being mine own, at length affection would
Thy blemishes amend, if so I could.
I wash’d thy face, but more defects I saw,
And rubbing off a spot, still made a flaw.
I stretcht thy joints to make thee even feet,
Yet still thou run’st more hobbling than is meet.
In better dress to trim thee was my mind,
But nought save home-spun Cloth, i’ th’ house I find.

options: The speaker lists the faults she sees in a child and then resolves to discipline the child more strictly.
The speaker regrets having allowed her book to be printed and then promises to revise it before it is printed again.
The speaker recounts her efforts to improve something she has made and then acknowledges a limit on what she can do.
The speaker praises the simple materials available in her home and then contrasts them with the finery she once owned.

passage: Italian-born Brazilian architect Lina Bo Bardi championed what she called “poor architecture,” meaning not poverty but the pursuit of maximum dignity and communication through minimal, humble means rather than costly materials or ornament. Her SESC Pompéia, a leisure center in São Paulo completed in stages between 1977 and 1986, exemplifies that approach. Rather than demolish the disused steel-drum factory on the site, Bo Bardi stripped away its plaster to expose the rough concrete beneath, preserved the sheds where neighborhood residents were already playing soccer and staging plays, and linked them by aerial walkways to new concrete towers.

options: It describes a dispute over whether an old factory should be preserved, then explains how that dispute was settled.

It sets out an architect’s guiding principle, then recounts the objections critics raised to a building based on it.
It introduces an idea about what architecture should aim for, then discusses a project that embodies that idea.

passage: Citizen science projects such as eBird, to which birdwatchers submit lists of the species they see, and NestWatch, in which volunteers record how many eggs are laid and hatched in active nests, enlist members of the public to gather data for scientific research. Both are what researchers call contributory projects: scientists design the study, and participants mainly supply observations. In co-created projects, by contrast, scientists and members of the public design the study together, and at least some participants take part in most or all stages of the research, from posing questions to interpreting and sharing results.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes two research projects that rely on volunteers, then explains why one has attracted more participants than the other.
It characterizes a kind of research by citing two projects, then describes a category of such research in which the public’s role is broader.
It presents two examples of citizen science, then argues that projects designed by scientists yield more reliable data than those designed with the public.
It traces the history of public participation in science, then proposes a new way of recruiting volunteers.

passage: The open ocean may harbor as many as a million undescribed species, but many of its inhabitants, among them jellyfish and squid, are soft-bodied, and the underwater equipment available for collecting them, much of it designed for the rough work of ocean mining and construction, frequently damages or destroys such animals before they can be studied. Zhi Ern Teoh and colleagues at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute addressed this difficulty with the rotary-actuated dodecahedron (RAD) sampler: driven by a single motor, its five 3D-printed petals fold into a hollow, twelve-sided enclosure that gently surrounds an organism and can reopen to release it unharmed.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a common belief about ocean life, then describes an expedition that disproved that belief.

It describes a difficulty in collecting some marine animals, then outlines a device designed to overcome that difficulty.
It explains how a sampling device was invented, then reports the new species that researchers discovered with it.

passage: Modern crocodilians and birds, the closest living relatives of non-avian dinosaurs, lay hard-shelled eggs, and paleontologists long assumed on that basis that non-avian dinosaurs did as well. A 2020 study led by Mark Norell of the American Museum of Natural History suggests otherwise. Chemical and microscopic analyses of unusually well-preserved eggs of Protoceratops, from Mongolia, and Mussaurus, from Argentina, showed that their shells had originally been soft, and comparisons with the eggshells of other reptiles indicated that the first dinosaurs laid soft eggs, with hard shells evolving independently at least three times.

options: It explains the basis for a long-held assumption, then reports research that calls that assumption into question.

It notes a disagreement between two teams of paleontologists, then explains how a new analysis settled it.

passage:
The following text is from John Keats’s 1817 poem “Sleep and Poetry.” Just before this passage, the speaker describes the kind of poetry he hopes will flourish.

Will not some say that I presumptuously
Have spoken? that from hastening disgrace
’T were better far to hide my foolish face?
That whining boyhood should with reverence bow
Ere the dread thunderbolt could reach [me]? How!
If I do hide myself, it sure shall be
In the very fane [temple], the light of Poesy:
If I do fall, at least I will be laid
Beneath the silence of a poplar shade;
And over me the grass shall be smooth shaven;
And there shall be a kind memorial graven.

passage:
The following text is from Henry James’s 1880 novel Washington Square. Dr. Austin Sloper is a physician in New York City in the first half of the nineteenth century.

It was an element in Dr. Sloper’s reputation that his learning and his skill were very evenly balanced; he was what you might call a scholarly doctor, and yet there was nothing abstract in his remedies—he always ordered you to take something. Though [Dr. Sloper] was felt to be extremely thorough, he was not uncomfortably theoretic, and if he sometimes explained matters rather more minutely than might seem of use to the patient, he never went so far (like some practitioners one has heard of) as to trust to the explanation alone, but always left behind him an inscrutable prescription.

passage: How do Saharan silver ants (Cataglyphis bombycina) forage in the full midday sun, when the desert surface can reach 70°C, while keeping their bodies below a critical thermal maximum of 53.6°C? Norman Nan Shi, Nanfang Yu, and their colleagues suggest that the answer lies in the dense coat of hairs that gives the ants their silvery sheen. Examining the hairs by electron microscopy, the team found that their triangular cross-sections make them highly reflective of the visible and near-infrared light in which sunlight is concentrated while also enhancing the ants’ emission of mid-infrared radiation, which lets them shed excess body heat toward the cooler sky.

The text presents a hypothesis about an insect’s coloring, then describes an experiment showing that the hypothesis was mistaken.

passage: Swedish traffic safety researcher Astrid Linder has criticized vehicle safety regulations for assessing occupant protection with crash test dummies based on an average-sized man, a figure whose stature and mass correspond to those of a woman larger than roughly 90 percent of women. Seats engineered around such dummies, Linder and her colleagues argue, protect women less effectively against whiplash, an injury for which women’s risk is up to three times that of men even in comparable collisions. As coordinator of ADSEAT, a European research project, Linder oversaw the development of EvaRID, a computational dummy representing an average-sized woman in rear-impact tests.

passage: Musicologist Eileen Southern, whose doctoral research concerned Renaissance music, became in the 1970s the first Black woman appointed a tenured full professor at Harvard University. Her book The Music of Black Americans: A History (1971), written partly in response to a colleague’s dismissive question about whether Black music comprised anything besides jazz, surveyed the full gamut of genres to which African Americans had contributed over some 450 years. Although earlier writers had interpreted individual aspects of that music, Southern’s history was the first comprehensive scholarly treatment of the subject, and it opened a vast new area of academic inquiry.

passage: Never Alone (Kisima Inŋitchuŋa), a 2014 puzzle-platform video game, was developed by Upper One Games, a company owned by the Cook Inlet Tribal Council, in partnership with some forty Alaska Native elders, storytellers, and community members. Adapting the traditional Iñupiaq tale “Kunuuksaayuka,” the game alternates control between a girl named Nuna and an Arctic fox and, as players progress, unlocks “cultural insights”: short documentary videos in which Iñupiat elders and storytellers share their stories. Reviewing the game for GameSpot, Daniel Hindes credited those videos with supplying valuable cultural context but faulted its sluggish, imprecise controls.

passage: In May 2015, more than 200,000 saiga antelopes, over 60 percent of the species’ global population, died within three weeks in central Kazakhstan, killed by hemorrhagic septicemia caused by the bacterium Pasteurella multocida. A contagion passed from animal to animal is an improbable cause, since entire calving aggregations sickened almost simultaneously. Nor was the pathogen a recent arrival: nearly identical strains have long persisted in apparently healthy saigas. More plausible is the account of Richard Kock of the Royal Veterinary College and colleagues, who link the event to unusually high humidity and heat, conditions associated with outbreaks of the disease in other animals.

passage: Searching Kepler data for additional planets around stars hosting hot Jupiters, gas giants that orbit their stars in a few days, Jason Steffen and colleagues found no sign of any, an absence readily explained if, as many astronomers think, such planets reach their orbits through high-eccentricity migration, an inward passage along a highly elongated path that would destabilize or engulf smaller neighbors. Later analyses confirmed that hot Jupiters almost never have close companions. WASP-47b, flanked by a super-Earth and a Neptune-sized planet, is a striking exception, which Chelsea Huang and colleagues attribute to its having formed near its present orbit, without such migration.
